f:adr: A US-traded security that stands for shares of a foreign company held by a depositary bank.
f:after-hours: Trading outside the regular US session of 9:30 a.m.
f:analyst-actions: What an analyst does to a rating.
f:average-price-target: The average of the price targets published by the analysts a data provider tracks.
f:backlog: Signed orders or contracts not yet delivered, and so not yet counted as revenue.
f:basis-points: A percentage point (pp) is the plain difference between two percentages; a basis point (bp) is one hundredth of a percentage point.
f:bear-market: By convention, a correction is a fall of 10% or more from a recent high, and a bear market a fall of 20% or more.
f:beat-miss: A beat is a result above the consensus estimate; a miss is below it.
f:beta: How much a stock has tended to move when the market moves: 1 means in step, above 1 bigger swings, below 1 smaller.
f:bid-ask-spread: The gap between the highest price a buyer offers (bid) and the lowest a seller accepts (ask).
f:blockchain: A shared record of transactions kept in copies by many independent computers (nodes).
f:bond-yield: The yearly return a bond pays at today's price.
f:breakeven-inflation: An ordinary Treasury yield minus the TIPS real yield of the same maturity: the average yearly inflation at which the two pay the same.
f:broker-ratings: Overweight, Outperform, Neutral and other house ratings
Firms' own rating words, which US rules require each firm to sort into Buy, Hold and Sell.
f:bull-bear-case: The bull case is the argument for the stock doing well; the bear case, the argument against.
f:buyback: A company buying its own shares on the market, which cuts the share count so each remaining share owns more of the profits.
f:cagr: The steady yearly growth rate that would turn a starting value into an ending value over a number of years.
f:call-option: A contract that gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy something at a set price (the strike) until or on a set date.
f:callable: A bond or preferred share the issuer can buy back early, at a set price after a set date.
f:cap-rate: A property's yearly net operating income (rent less operating costs, before loan payments) divided by its value or price.
f:capex: Money spent on long-lasting assets such as factories, equipment, networks or data centers.
f:catalyst: A known or expected event that could move the share price, such as an earnings report, product launch, court ruling, regulatory decision or index change.
f:cet1-ratio: A bank's highest-quality capital, mainly common equity and retained earnings, as a percentage of its risk-weighted assets: loans and other holdings, each scaled by how risky it is.
f:combined-ratio: An insurer's claims plus expenses as a percentage of the premiums it earned.
f:company-size: Rough size bands by market cap, with no official lines.
f:consensus-estimate: The average forecast of the analysts covering a company, for revenue, EPS or another figure, for a coming quarter or year.
f:consensus-rating: The average of the ratings given by the analysts who cover the stock, expressed as one word on a scale from Strong Sell to Strong Buy.
f:contango: A futures market is in contango when later delivery months cost more than nearer ones, usually because holding the thing costs money.
f:cost-of-carry: Cost of carry and fair value
The cost of holding something over time: interest on the money tied up, plus storage and insurance, less income such as dividends.
f:coupon: The fixed yearly interest a bond pays, as a percentage of its face value, usually in two payments a year.
f:credit-rating: A rating agency's grade of a borrower's ability to repay, from AAA (Aaa at Moody's) downward.
f:crypto-supply: Circulating supply, max supply and crypto market cap
Circulating supply is the coins issued so far; max supply is the protocol's hard limit, if any: 21 million for bitcoin, none for ETH.
f:cryptocurrency: Digital money recorded on a blockchain, with no bank or government issuing it.
f:currency-hedged: A fund that uses contracts to cancel most of the effect of exchange-rate moves on its foreign holdings, so its return tracks the assets in the investor's own currency.
f:current-ratio: Assets that turn into cash within a year against bills due within a year: a test of short-term liquidity.
f:cyclical: A cyclical business rises and falls with the economy (carmakers, chips, steel, airlines); a defensive one sells what people buy regardless (food, utilities, medicines).
f:debt-to-equity: Borrowings compared with the shareholders' stake in the company.
f:depreciation: An expense that spreads the cost of a long-lived asset, such as a machine or a building, over the years it is used; amortization does the same for intangible assets.
f:dilution: When a company issues new shares, through stock-based pay, acquisitions or fundraising, each existing share owns a smaller slice.
f:distribution-yield: A fund's cash payouts as a percentage of its price.
f:dividend: Cash a company pays its shareholders out of profits, usually every quarter in the US.
f:dividend-yield: A year's dividends per share as a percentage of the share price: the cash income each dollar invested brings in before tax, if the dividend stays the same.
f:dollar-index: ICE's index of the US dollar against six currencies, weighted 57.6% euro, 13.6% yen, 11.9% pound, 9.1% Canadian dollar, 4.2% Swedish krona and 3.6% Swiss franc.
f:dot-plot: A chart in the Fed's Summary of Economic Projections, published four times a year, showing participants' views of the right federal funds rate at the end of the next few years and in the longer run, without names.
f:dow: One of the oldest US stock-market averages, running since 1896: 30 large US companies chosen by a committee.
f:drawdown: A fall from a previous high, in percent.
f:duration: Modified duration is roughly the percent a bond's price moves, the opposite way, for a 1 percentage point change in yield.
f:earnings-call: Each quarter a company publishes its results, the earnings release or 'print', and management takes analysts' questions on a conference call.
f:ebitda: Operating profit before the non-cash charges for the wearing out of assets (depreciation and amortization), and before interest and taxes.
f:efficiency-ratio: A bank's operating costs as a share of its revenue; lower means leaner.
f:enterprise-value: The value of the whole business to everyone with a claim on it: the stock-market value plus debt, minus cash.
f:eps: The company's profit over the last 12 months divided by its number of shares: the year's profit that belongs to each share.
f:etf: A fund whose shares trade on a stock exchange throughout the day, like a company's shares.
f:ev-ebitda: The value of the whole business, debt included, divided by its yearly operating earnings before depreciation.
f:exchange: The marketplace where a stock is listed and traded.
f:expense-ratio: A fund's yearly running costs as a percentage of its assets, taken out of the fund's value rather than billed.
f:fiscal-year: A company's 12-month accounting year, which need not match the calendar.
f:float: Shares outstanding are all the shares a company has issued to investors.
f:fomc: The Federal Reserve committee that sets the target range for the federal funds rate and decides on the Fed's bond holdings.
f:forward-guidance: What a central bank says about the likely path of its policy rate.
f:forward-pe: The share price divided by the earnings per share analysts expect over the coming year.
f:free-cash-flow: The cash a business generated after paying its running costs and its investment in equipment, buildings and the like.
f:futures-contract: An exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a set amount of something, such as oil, a stock index or a currency, on a future date at a price fixed today.
f:gaap: GAAP are the US accounting rules behind US companies' filings; many companies abroad use IFRS, the international rules, instead.
f:gic: A Canadian deposit that pays a set rate for a fixed term, from a few months to several years, usually with the money locked in until it matures.
f:goc-bond: A loan to the Canadian federal government that pays fixed interest every six months.
f:greeks: Measures of how an option's price responds to the stock, time and volatility.
f:gross-margin: The share of each sales dollar left after the direct cost of making or buying what was sold.
f:guidance: Management's own forecast for coming results, usually revenue, margins or EPS for the next quarter or year, given alongside earnings.
f:hyperscaler: One of the few companies that run data centers at vast scale, for cloud services or their own apps: Amazon, Microsoft and Google, often with Meta and Oracle counted in.
f:impairment: Goodwill is the premium paid in an acquisition above the value of the assets bought.
f:implied-volatility: The volatility that makes an option-pricing model, such as Black-Scholes, match an option's market price: the market's own estimate of how much the price will swing, as a yearly percentage.
f:index-fund: A fund that copies an index instead of picking stocks, usually by holding its members in the index's proportions (full replication).
f:insider: A company's officers and directors and anyone owning more than 10% of its shares.
f:institutional-investors: Organizations that invest large pools of money for others: fund managers, pension funds, insurers.
f:ipo: A company's first sale of shares to the public, and the start of trading on an exchange.
f:iron-condor: Option combinations that profit if a price ends inside a range.
f:leverage: Leverage is the use of borrowed money.
f:ma-200: The average closing price over the last 200 trading days, about ten months.
f:ma-50: The average closing price over the last 50 trading days, about ten weeks.
f:margin-call: A demand to add cash to a margin account.
f:margin-expansion: Margin expansion is a rising share of revenue kept as profit.
f:mark-to-market: Valuing a position at today's market price.
f:market-cap: What the stock market values the whole company at: the share price times the number of shares.
f:market-maker: A firm that quotes prices to buy and sell all day and earns the gap between them, the bid-ask spread.
f:mer: The Canadian measure of a fund's yearly cost: management fee plus operating expenses and taxes, as a percentage of assets.
f:moat: A lasting advantage that keeps competitors from taking a company's profits, like a moat around a castle.
f:money-market-fund: A fund that holds very short-term, high-quality debt such as Treasury bills and pays interest close to short-term rates; most aim to keep a steady unit price.
f:moving-average: The average of the last several closing prices, recalculated each period, so the line smooths out short-term swings and shows the trend.
f:multiple: A multiple is a price divided by a measure of the business, such as P/E, EV/EBITDA or price-to-sales (market cap ÷ revenue).
f:nasdaq-100: An index of the 100 largest companies listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange, leaving out banks and other financial companies.
f:nav: Net asset value per share: the fund's assets minus liabilities, divided by its shares, set once a day.
f:net-assets: The total value of everything a fund owns minus what it owes: the size of the fund.
f:net-debt-to-ebitda: How many years of operating earnings it would take to repay debt net of cash.
f:net-interest-margin: A bank's core spread: interest earned on loans and securities minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings, as a share of the assets that earn interest.
f:net-profit-margin: The share of sales that ends up as profit after every cost, interest payment and tax: the bottom line as a percentage of the top line.
f:one-off-items: Gains or charges that won't repeat, such as a legal fine, an asset sale or a write-down.
f:open-interest: The number of futures or options contracts still open at the end of a day: positions opened and not yet closed or expired.
f:operating-cash-flow: The cash a company's day-to-day business generates in a period: net income adjusted for items that use no cash, such as depreciation, and for changes in working capital such as receivables and inventory.
f:operating-margin: The share of sales left after all running costs, including research, marketing and administration, but before interest and taxes.
f:organic-growth: Organic growth leaves out revenue added by acquisitions or lost by selling businesses.
f:payout-ratio: The share of profit paid out as dividends.
f:peg-ratio: The P/E divided by the expected yearly growth rate of earnings, in percent.
f:policy-rate: The short-term interest rate a central bank sets: the federal funds target range in the US (the Federal Reserve) and the overnight rate in Canada (the Bank of Canada).
f:preferred-share: A class of share that usually pays a fixed dividend and ranks ahead of common shares for dividends and in a wind-up, but behind lenders.
f:price-target: An analyst's estimate of where the share price will be, usually 12 months out.
f:price-to-book: The share price against book value per share, the accounting value of what shareholders own (assets minus liabilities).
f:proof-of-stake: A way of adding blocks in which validators lock up (stake) the network's coins as a security deposit instead of mining.
f:proof-of-work: Bitcoin's way of adding blocks: miners race to solve a computing puzzle, and the winner earns new coins (the block subsidy) plus fees.
f:put-option: A contract that gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell something at a set price (the strike) until or on a set date.
f:rate-base: For a regulated utility, the rate base is the value of its network (plants, wires, pipes) on which regulators let it earn a return.
f:rating-scale: Strong Buy, Buy, Hold, Sell, Strong Sell
The common five-step scale for analysts' ratings.
f:reit: A company that owns or finances income-producing property.
f:retained-earnings: The total of a company's profits over its life, less its losses and the dividends it has paid, kept in the business.
f:revenue: The money a company takes in from selling its goods and services, before any costs.
f:revenue-growth: How much more, or less, the company sold than a year earlier, in percent.
f:roe: Profit as a percentage of the shareholders' stake (equity): how hard the owners' money is working.
f:roic: After-tax operating profit as a percentage of all the money invested in the business by lenders and shareholders alike.
f:roll: Closing a futures contract as it nears expiry and opening the same position in a later one, to keep the exposure going.
f:rotce: A bank's profit as a percentage of its tangible common equity: shareholders' equity minus goodwill, other intangibles and preferred stock.
f:rsi: A 0–100 gauge of how strongly a price has risen versus fallen over recent periods.
f:sales-load: A sales charge some mutual funds take when you buy (a front-end load) or sell (a back-end load, or deferred sales charge), on top of the yearly fee.
f:same-day-options: Options traded on the day they expire.
f:sec-filings: The SEC regulates US securities markets.
f:sec-yield: A standardized yield the SEC requires when a US bond or stock fund quotes a yield: income earned over the last 30 days, minus fund expenses, expressed as a yearly rate.
f:segment: A segment is a business line the company reports separately, such as Apple's iPhone or Services.
f:sell-side: A researcher at a bank or broker who follows a set of companies and publishes earnings forecasts, ratings and price targets for clients.
f:shareholders-equity: A company's assets minus its liabilities on the balance sheet: the owners' share of the books.
f:sharpe-ratio: The return earned above a risk-free rate, what short-term government bills pay, for each unit of volatility taken.
f:short-interest: Shares that investors have sold short, a bet that the price will fall, as a percentage of the shares available to trade (or of all shares).
f:sp-500: An index of about 500 large US companies, weighted by market value and chosen by a committee at S&P Dow Jones Indices.
f:spin-off: A company turns a division into a separate listed company and hands its shares to existing shareholders.
f:spot-crypto-etf: An exchange-traded fund that holds the cryptocurrency itself, kept by a custodian, so investors can own its price moves through an ordinary brokerage account.
f:stablecoin: A crypto token built to hold a steady value, usually one US dollar, typically backed by cash and short-term Treasury bills held by its issuer.
f:stock-split: A split divides each share into several, lowering the price per share without changing the company's value; a reverse split combines shares.
f:straddle: A straddle is a call and a put at the same strike and expiry; a strangle uses a call with a higher strike and a put with a lower one.
f:strike-price: The price at which an option's holder can buy (a call) or sell (a put).
f:tam: The total yearly spending on a product category: the most a company could sell if it had every customer.
f:tips: TIPS are Treasury securities whose principal rises and falls with consumer prices (the CPI-U index), so the coupon is paid on an inflation-adjusted amount.
f:total-return: The gain from the price change plus dividends, assuming each dividend is reinvested.
f:trailing-pe: How many dollars investors pay for each dollar of the company's profit over the last 12 months.
f:treasury-auction: Treasury sells new debt at auction: every winning bidder pays one price, set by the highest accepted yield.
f:treasury-bill: A US government loan of a year or less with no coupon: it sells below face value and repays face value at maturity, and the difference is the interest.
f:treasury-note-bond: Loans to the US government that pay fixed interest every six months and repay face value at maturity: notes run 2 to 10 years, bonds 20 or 30 years.
f:ttm: The four most recently reported quarters added together.
f:vertical-spread: Buying one option and selling another of the same type and expiry at a different strike.
f:vix: Cboe's index of the volatility S&P 500 options are pricing over the next 30 days, as a yearly percentage.
f:volatility: How widely returns swing around their average, measured as the standard deviation of returns and usually scaled to a yearly figure.
f:yield-to-maturity: The yearly return from buying a bond at today's price and holding it to maturity, counting every coupon and the repayment of face value, with coupons reinvested at the same rate.
f:yoy: Year over year (YoY) compares a period with the same period a year earlier, which removes seasonal swings.
p:actions: The five things a player can do when it is their turn: check, bet, call, raise or fold.
p:advantage-play: Methods that turn a game to a player edge by exploiting how it is run: card counting, hole-carding, full-pay video poker with cash-back, progressives near their ceiling.
p:all-in: Betting every chip you have on the table, which no-limit games allow at any time.
p:angle-shoot: Using tricks that skirt the rules to mislead opponents, such as acting as if to fold or hiding large chips behind small ones.
p:ante: A forced bet posted before the deal on top of the blinds, by every player or, in many tournaments, by the big blind for the whole table; common in later tournament stages.
p:ante-bonus: An extra payout on the Three Card Poker Ante for a straight or better, paid whether or not you beat the dealer.
p:bad-beat: Losing a hand you were a strong favorite to win when an opponent catches a long-shot card.
p:banker-bet: The baccarat bet on the hand that draws last.
p:bankroll: Money set aside for gambling, apart from money needed for anything else.
p:basic-strategy: The mathematically best play for every player hand against every dealer upcard, given the table's rules.
p:bet: Put chips in first in a betting round; before the flop the big blind counts as that bet.
p:betting-system: A rule for changing bet size based on past results, such as Martingale: double after every loss.
p:big-6-big-8: A bet that 6 (or 8) rolls before a 7, paid even money.
p:blackjack-side-bets: Optional bets on the first cards dealt.
p:blackjack-switch: Two hands of equal size, with the right to swap their second cards.
p:blinds: Forced bets posted before the deal by the two players to the left of the button: the small blind and the big blind, usually twice as large.
p:bluff: A bet or raise with a weak hand that wins only if opponents fold.
p:bust: Going over 21, which loses at once.
p:button: A disc marking the player in the dealer's position for the hand; it moves one seat to the left after every hand.
p:buy-bet: A place bet paid at true odds, less a 5% commission charged either when it wins or when the bet goes down.
p:call: Match the current bet to stay in the hand.
p:card-counting: Tracking dealt cards to know when the rest of the shoe is rich in tens and aces, which favors the player, and betting more then.
p:carnival-game: A table game, often poker-flavored, played against the dealer with fixed rules and paytables, such as Ultimate Texas Hold'em and Three Card Poker.
p:cash-game: Poker played for the chips on the table, which stand for real money.
p:check: Pass without betting and keep your cards, allowed only while no one has bet in the round.
p:come-bet: Pass and don't pass bets made after the point is set.
p:come-out-roll: The first roll of a new round.
p:commission-free-baccarat: Versions that drop the 5% Banker commission and instead make a winning Banker three-card 7 a push.
p:community-cards: The face-up cards in the middle of the table that every player can use, five in hold'em, together called the board.
p:comps: Rewards a casino gives players based on how much they bet: points, cash-back, meals, rooms.
p:continuation-bet: A bet on the flop by the player who made the last raise before it, continuing to represent a strong hand whether or not the flop helped.
p:cooler: A hand in which two very strong hands meet and the loser couldn't reasonably have folded, such as a full house against four of a kind.
p:cost-per-hour: What a game costs in expectation for an hour of play: the house edge times the bet times the decisions per hour.
p:dealer-qualifies: The minimum hand the dealer needs: a pair in Ultimate Texas Hold'em, queen-high in Three Card Poker.
p:degen: Short for degenerate gambler: someone who will bet on anything, at any odds, usually more than is wise.
p:deuces-wild: A video poker game in which every 2 is wild and stands for any card.
p:dice-control: The claim that a practiced grip and soft throw can make 7s rarer than 1 roll in 6.
p:dont-pass: The bet against the shooter: on the come-out, 2 or 3 wins, 12 pushes (the bar 12), and 7 or 11 loses; after that it wins if a 7 comes before the point.
p:double-down: Doubling your bet in exchange for exactly one more card.
p:double-exposure: Both dealer cards are dealt face up.
p:double-zero-wheel: A wheel with 38 pockets: 1 to 36, a zero and a double zero.
p:drawdown: The largest drop from a high point to a later low within a session: how deep a bankroll sinks before it recovers or play ends.
p:edge-sorting: Reading tiny asymmetries in the printed backs of cards, after getting the dealer to turn the high cards around, to tell high from low before betting.
p:element-of-risk: The house edge measured against all the money a player puts at risk in a round, not just the first bet.
p:equity: Your share of the pot on average: the chance your hand wins, counting split pots as part-wins, if all the remaining cards were dealt with no more betting.
p:expected-value: The average result of a decision if it could be repeated many times: each outcome times its probability, added up.
p:exploitative-play: Departing from balanced play to profit from one opponent's habits: bluffing a player who folds too often, value betting one who calls too much.
p:field: A one-roll bet that wins on 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11 or 12 and loses on 5, 6, 7 or 8.
p:first-base: The first seat to the dealer's left, which acts first, and the last seat, which acts just before the dealer.
p:fish: A weak player who loses money over time, often without knowing it.
p:five-number-bet: A bet on 0, 00, 1, 2 and 3 on a double-zero wheel, paying 6 to 1.
p:fold: Give up the hand and any chips already in the pot; the cards go into the muck, the pile of discards.
p:fold-equity: The part of a bet's value that comes from the chance opponents fold.
p:free-bet-blackjack: The house funds free doubles on hard 9, 10 or 11 and free splits of any pair but tens, marked with a lammer: a win is paid on it, a loss costs only your own bet.
p:free-odds: An extra bet behind a pass, come, don't pass or don't come bet once it has a number, paid at true odds: the only bet in the casino with no house edge.
p:full-pay: A machine carrying the best common version of its game's paytable, such as 9/6 Jacks or Better; a short-pay machine has one or more lines cut.
p:gamblers-fallacy: The belief that past independent results change the next one: that red is due after a run of black, that a hot shooter will keep making points, or that a baccarat scorecard shows a pattern.
p:grinder: A player who earns a modest, steady edge through long hours and volume, closer to an office job than an adventure.
p:gto: A strategy no opponent can profit against by changing their own play, approximated in practice by solver software.
p:hand-rankings: The order of five-card poker hands, highest first: royal flush, straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair, high card.
p:hardways: A bet that 4, 6, 8 or 10 rolls as a pair, such as 3 + 3 for hard 6, before it rolls any other way (the easy way) or a 7 shows.
p:heater: A winning streak better than skill alone would explain.
p:hit-frequency: The share of plays that return anything at all.
p:hit-stand: The two basic choices: hit takes another card, stand keeps your total and ends your turn.
p:hold: The share of money played that a machine keeps over time, the slot version of house edge; a loose machine holds less, a tight one more.
p:hole-carding: Seeing a dealer's face-down card that a careless dealer exposes.
p:hole-cards: Your private, face-down cards: two in Texas hold'em.
p:house-edge: The share of each bet the casino keeps on average over the long run, built in by paying winners less than the true odds.
p:icm: A model that converts tournament chip stacks into shares of the prize pool.
p:implied-odds: Pot odds plus the money you expect to win on later streets if you hit.
p:index-plays: Departures from basic strategy at set true counts, such as standing on 16 against a 10 at a true count of 0 or higher.
p:inside-bets: Bets on the numbered grid: a single number pays 35 to 1, a split (two adjacent numbers) 17 to 1, a corner (four numbers) 8 to 1.
p:insurance: A side bet, offered when the dealer shows an ace, that the hidden card is a ten.
p:jacks-or-better: The base video poker game: a pair of jacks or higher returns your bet, two pair returns 2 coins per coin bet, and so on up to the royal flush at 800 per coin with five coins in.
p:kicker: A side card outside a hand's pair, two pair, trips or quads that still counts in the best five cards.
p:la-partage: Single-zero rules for even-money bets when the ball lands on zero: under la partage you lose only half the bet; under en prison the bet stays on the table for the next spin.
p:law-of-large-numbers: Over many independent bets, the average result per bet settles toward its expected value.
p:lay-bet: A bet that a 7 rolls before a chosen number, paid at true odds less 5% of the win.
p:losses-disguised-as-wins: A spin that pays back less than it cost but plays the winning sounds anyway: bet $2, win $0.60.
p:max-coins: Betting the full five coins per hand.
p:mini-baccarat: The same game at a smaller table, with the dealer handling every card: 120–150 hands an hour against about 40 at the big table, where players squeeze cards to reveal them slowly.
p:natural: An ace and a ten-value card as your first two cards: a two-card 21.
p:near-miss: Two jackpot symbols on the payline and the third just off it.
p:nine-six: Shorthand for a Jacks or Better paytable: what it pays per coin for a full house and for a flush.
p:nit: A very tight, cautious player who plays only premium hands and rarely bluffs.
p:nuts: The best possible hand given the cards on the board.
p:optimal-strategy: The hold for every dealt hand that maximizes a machine's long-run return, given its paytable.
p:outs: The unseen cards that would turn your hand into one that probably wins.
p:outside-bets: Bets on groups of numbers around the grid: red or black, odd or even, and high or low pay even money; a dozen or a column pays 2 to 1.
p:pair-plus: Three Card Poker's separate bet on your own three cards, ignoring the dealer: a pair pays 1 to 1, a straight flush 40 to 1.
p:pass-line: The bet with the shooter: wins on a come-out 7 or 11 or a made point; loses on a come-out 2, 3 or 12 or a 7 before the point.
p:payline: A line across the reels on which matching symbols pay.
p:paytable: The printed schedule of what each result pays.
p:penetration: How far into the shoe the dealer deals before reshuffling, marked by a cut card.
p:place-bet: A bet that a chosen number rolls before a 7, with no come-out needed.
p:player-bet: The baccarat bet on the hand that draws first, paid even money with no commission.
p:point: The number, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10, set by the come-out roll.
p:position: Where you sit relative to the button, which sets the order of action.
p:pot-odds: The price the pot offers on a call: what you stand to win against what it costs.
p:progressive-jackpot: A jackpot that grows by a slice of every bet until someone hits it, funded by the players who don't.
p:proposition-bets: Long-shot bets in the middle of the layout, mostly settled in one roll: any seven, any craps (2, 3 or 12), a single 2, 3, 11 or 12, and bundles such as the horn (2, 3, 11, 12) and C and E (craps and eleven).
p:push: A tie between player and dealer: the bet is returned, neither won nor lost.
p:push-22: The rule behind Free Bet Blackjack and Blackjack Switch: a dealer total of 22 ties every player hand still standing instead of busting.
p:q-6-4: The whole Three Card Poker strategy: play any hand of queen-six-four or better, fold anything worse.
p:raise: Increase the current bet, so the others must match the new amount to stay in.
p:rake: The card room's fee for running a poker game: a cut of each pot, a charge per hour, or part of a tournament entry.
p:range: The full set of hands an opponent could hold given their actions so far, instead of a single guess.
p:risk-of-ruin: The chance of losing an entire bankroll before reaching a goal or the end of play.
p:rng: The software that picks a slot's result the instant you press the button.
p:rounder: A player who makes a living from poker by making the rounds of games, traveling wherever the action is.
p:rtp: The share of money bet that a game pays back over the long run: 100% minus the house edge.
p:rule-of-2-and-4: A quick estimate of the chance of hitting one of your outs: multiply the outs by 4 when you will see two more cards, or by 2 when you will see one.
p:run-good: Results above or below expectation because of the cards, not the decisions.
p:s17-h17: Whether the dealer stands on a soft 17 (S17) or hits it (H17); the felt says which.
p:sample-size: How many hands, bets or sessions a result rests on.
p:semi-bluff: A bet with a draw: a hand that is probably behind now but has outs to become the best.
p:seven-out: A 7 rolled after a point is set.
p:shark: A strong player who wins by finding weaker ones and playing against them.
p:shoe: The box several decks are dealt from, typically six to eight in blackjack and eight in baccarat.
p:showdown: The end of a hand when two or more players remain after the last betting round: the hands are turned face up and the best one takes the pot.
p:side-bet: An optional extra wager beside the main bet, paid from its own paytable.
p:side-pot: A separate pot built from bets an all-in player can't match.
p:single-zero-wheel: A roulette wheel with 37 pockets: 1 to 36 plus one green zero.
p:soft-and-hard: A soft hand counts an ace as 11 and can't bust on the next card, such as ace-6, a soft 17.
p:spanish-21: Blackjack with the four tens removed from each deck (face cards stay), worth about 2% to the house, given back through rules and bonuses: player 21 always wins, late surrender, doubling on any number of cards.
p:split: Turning a starting pair into two separate hands, each with its own bet equal to the first.
p:standard-deviation: Variance in money terms: the typical distance between a result and its expected value.
p:streets: The four betting rounds of hold'em, called streets.
p:string-bet: Putting chips in with more than one forward motion without first announcing a raise.
p:super-fun-21: Usually single deck, with many gifts, such as surrender after doubling and an automatic win for six cards totaling 20 or less, paid for by one rule: blackjack pays even money, except in diamonds, where it pays 2 to 1.
p:surrender: Giving up a hand after the first two cards and getting half the bet back.
p:tcp-ante-play: The main game: post an Ante, see three cards, then fold or Play by adding an equal bet.
p:texas-holdem: The standard form of poker in card rooms and tournaments.
p:third-card-rule: Baccarat hands count only the last digit of their total (7 + 8 = 15 = 5), tens and pictures as zero; closest to nine wins.
p:tie-bet: The baccarat bet that Banker and Player finish level.
p:tilt: Playing worse because emotion has taken over, usually after a bad beat or a losing run: chasing losses, betting bigger, calling when you know better.
p:tournament: Players pay a fixed entry and get tournament chips with no cash value.
p:trips: Ultimate Texas Hold'em's optional side bet, paid on your own final hand, three of a kind or better, whatever the dealer holds.
p:true-count: The running count (the total of the count values of every card seen since the shuffle) divided by the decks left to deal.
p:true-odds: True odds are the real chance of a result, as ways to lose against ways to win; payout odds are what the casino pays.
p:upcard: The dealer's face-up card; the other, face down, is the hole card.
p:uth-ante-blind: Two equal bets every player posts before the deal.
p:uth-play-bet: The one decision in Ultimate Texas Hold'em: raise 4x or 3x the ante before the flop, 2x after it, or 1x after the river, else fold.
p:value-bet: A bet made to be called by worse hands, where a bluff hopes better hands fold.
p:variance: How widely results scatter around the expected value.
p:video-poker: Five-card draw on a machine: five cards from a fair 52-card deck, hold any, replace the rest once, and get paid on the final hand from a paytable printed on the glass.
p:vig: A fee taken out of a bet or its winnings, instead of being built into the payout.
p:volatility: How a game's payback is spread across its outcomes.
p:whale: A player who bets very large amounts, at poker or in the casino.
p:wheel-bias: A physical flaw, such as a loose fret or a slight tilt, that makes some numbers come up more often than chance.
